messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Teacher
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Vignette:
Rukmini, a 31-year-old South Asian woman, had always been passionate about teaching. She loved nothing more than seeing her students learn and grow, and her enthusiasm was contagious. But all of that changed on the day she accidentally caused serious injury to one of her students during a science experiment gone wrong. The incident happened over two years ago, but for Rukmini, it feels like just yesterday. The memory of that day is still seared in her mind - she can smell the acrid scent of burning chemicals and hear the sound of shattering glass. It's as if time froze, and all she can recall are snapshots of moments: the look of horror on her student's face, the feeling of helplessness as she tried to stop the bleeding, and the eerie silence that followed. Even now, when she thinks about it, Rukmini is transported back to that moment, and it feels like it's happening all over again. Since then, Rukmini has struggled with feelings of self-blame and inadequacy. She can't shake off the thought that if only she had been more careful, more attentive, the accident wouldn't have happened. She's convinced that her actions were directly responsible for the harm caused to her student. As a result, she feels like she's lost her identity as a teacher - something that defined her and gave her purpose. Rukmini has come to believe that she's no longer capable of doing what she loves, and this realization fills her with despair. Rukmini's colleagues and friends have tried to reassure her, praising her for her dedication and care, but their words only make her feel worse. Being praised or receiving positive attention now triggers a sense of discomfort and guilt in her. She feels like an imposter, and the more people try to lift her up, the more she shrinks away. Even the smallest gesture of kindness can set off a wave of anxiety, leaving her feeling overwhelmed. Positive emotions have also become confusing for Rukmini. She can't understand why others seem so happy and carefree when she's still grappling with the weight of what happened. When someone talks about an accident or shares a story of near-miss, it sends Rukmini spiraling back to that fateful day. Conversations that used to be innocuous now feel like landmines waiting to trigger a memory or emotion that she can't handle. As time has passed, Rukmini's avoidance behaviors have taken on a life of their own. She's become increasingly withdrawn, skipping staff meetings and social events where she might encounter people who know about the accident. Her relationships with colleagues and friends have begun to fray, and her husband is growing concerned about her isolation. At work, Rukmini has started to rely more heavily on lesson plans and rigid routines, hoping that structure will somehow keep her safe from similar mistakes in the future. But despite her best efforts, Rukmini can't shake off the feeling of being an outsider - like she's no longer part of the community she once belonged to. She feels like a stranger in her own classroom, always on edge, waiting for the next disaster to strike. And when it doesn't, she's left with a hollow sense of relief that only serves to remind her of what happened before. It was only when Rukmini realized that she couldn't keep living in this state of suspended animation, constantly looking over her shoulder, waiting for the other shoe to drop, that she finally sought help. She hopes therapy will give her back some semblance of control over her life and emotions, but most of all, she's afraid of confronting the reality of what happened - and the person she's become as a result.
